title: Loss, Loyalty, and the Road Home
overview: After a famine, three deaths, and ten years abroad, the widow Naomi returns to Bethlehem with her foreign daughter-in-law Ruth, who refuses to leave her.

parts.label: Famine drives a family away (vv. 1-2)
parts.note: Bethlehem means "house of bread," so a famine there is a bitter irony, and this family moves to Moab, a neighboring nation east of the Dead Sea that was often at odds with Israel. Elimelech means "my God is king" and Naomi means "pleasant," while the sons' names may suggest sickness and frailty, though scholars are unsure.

parts.label: Death after death (vv. 3-5)
parts.note: Naomi loses her husband and then both sons, who had married local Moabite women and left no children. In that world a widow with no sons had no one to provide for or protect her, and the text gives no reason for these deaths.

parts.label: Naomi urges them home (vv. 6-14)
parts.note: Hearing the famine has ended, Naomi asks the LORD to treat her daughters-in-law kindly, using a Hebrew word for loyal, faithful love that becomes a thread through the whole book. Her talk of having more sons points to a custom where a dead man's brother married his widow to carry on his family, and she is telling them plainly she has no future to offer.

parts.label: Ruth refuses to leave (vv. 15-18)
parts.note: Orpah kisses Naomi goodbye and returns to her own people, and the story does not blame her, but Ruth binds herself to Naomi's people, God, and even her burial place. She seals it with a solemn oath in the LORD's name, which was a serious and binding way to make a promise.

parts.label: "Call me Mara" (vv. 19-22)
parts.note: Mara means "bitter," and Naomi openly says the Almighty has emptied her life, an honest complaint the text records without correcting. The two women arrive as the barley harvest begins, around March or April, a quiet hint that things may be about to change.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether the chapter implies the family's move to Moab and the sons' marriages were wrong and the deaths a punishment, or whether it simply tells of tragedy without passing judgment.
think: What do you think makes someone stay with a person who has lost everything, when leaving would be easier?
